full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are not in dispute and may be shortly stated. An application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act filed by opposite party No. 1 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh was allowed to be amended by an order dated 13.4.88. The petitioner who is the purchaser took an appeal there from to the learned District Judge of that place. As no appeal lies against an order allowing amendment of plaint/application the learned District Judge dismissed the same on 4.6.88. The unsuccessful petitioner without moving against the order of the Subordinate Judge, however, moved this court in Civil Revision No. 904 of 1988 and obtained a Rule thereon against the order of the learned District Judge. A Single Bench of this court discharged the Rule on 5.6.90. After a lapse of about two months and a half for which no explanation has been offered another revisional application was filed calling in question the propriety of the order of the Subordinate Judge allowing amendment of the application for pre-emption. The application contains a prayer for condonation of delay of 857 days. As it was out of time the same was returned to the learned Advocate for speedily moving the same before the court. That was, however not done until 16.9.90. 

 4. The pre-emptor opposite party opposed the prayer by filing an affidavit-in-opposition in which it is averred that the petitioner miserably failed to show sufficient cause for condonation of the delay. It is further stated therein that the petitioner also failed to explain the delay of 28 days that took place in between the date of affirmation of the affidavit in support of the revisional application and the actual date of moving the same in court. 

 7. Section 5 of the Limitation Act provides for condonation of delay when the applicant satisfies the court that he had sufficient cause for not preferring an appeal/application within the prescribed period. Mistaken advice of a lawyer may no doubt constitute sufficient cause in certain circumstances but one rule is firmly established that once the abnormal period of limitation is allowed to run out the applicant has to explain every day's delay beyond the period of limitation. Viewing the facts stated hereinabove in the light of the above settled principle I am unable to hold that the petitioner has been able to explain the long delay satisfactorily.
